body: You need a placeholder in some text you're working on; instead of lorem ipsum, why not just ask the LLM to generate some strawman text? Surely there can be no harm in that?

Danger, Will Robinson! Thinking about a problem changes you so that your future thoughts will invariably be influenced by your past thinking. This is particularly problematic if your first "thoughts" about the problem is not your own, but that of the LLM. Design research calls this phenomenon "design fixation", and is an old idea exacerbated by generative AI. I wrote about this in a blog post linked below.

title: I have an open Ph.D. position in my group at Aarhus University on the topic of coding agents for data visualization…
dek: Possible directions include natural language and multimodal interfaces for visualization authoring, human-AI collaboration patterns for iterative analysis, situated and context-aware analytics,…
body: I have an open Ph.D. position in my group at Aarhus University on the topic of coding agents for data visualization and analytics in ubiquitous, mobile, and field settings. Visualization today remains tethered to desktop environments and technical users. AI systems that generate, modify, and execute code on behalf of users offer a path toward visual data analysis for anyone, anywhere, on any device. The project asks how such agents should work on phones, tablets, and wearable displays; in the field, the clinic, or the classroom; and for analysts, domain experts, and citizens alike.

Possible directions include natural language and multimodal interfaces for visualization authoring, human-AI collaboration patterns for iterative analysis, situated and context-aware analytics, and maintaining transparency and user agency when AI mediates the entire pipeline from data to visual output. Immersive and extended reality platforms are also in scope.

The position starts November 2026 or later at the Department of Computer Science, Aarhus University. We follow participatory methods, working closely with domain experts and end-users, and combine system prototyping with qualitative studies and empirical evaluation. Funding is provided by my Villum Investigator grant---the Center for Anytime Anywhere Analytics (CA3)---by Villum Fonden.
Apply by August 1, 2026; more details here: https://lnkd.in/e_4ss5zM

title: Extra, extra, read all about our comparative study of three accessible data exploration systems for blind users: a…
dek: We found that task accuracy was comparable across all three systems, but completion time and perceived workload differed substantially. Participants were fastest on the Monarch tactile display.…
body: Extra, extra, read all about our comparative study of three accessible data exploration systems for blind users: a screen reader (Olli), an audio-tactile tablet (TactualPlot), and the Monarch refreshable tactile display. Ten blind participants completed data analysis tasks across bar charts, pie charts, line charts, and scatterplots.

We found that task accuracy was comparable across all three systems, but completion time and perceived workload differed substantially. Participants were fastest on the Monarch tactile display. Qualitative data revealed that the real differentiator isn't the sensory modality (sound vs. touch) but the specific device-level design choices and interaction techniques that operationalize these modalities in practice.
Excellent collaboration with Pramod Chundury, J. Bern Jordan, Yasmin Reyazuddin, and Jonathan Lazar. And thanks to American Printing House for the Blind for lending us the Monarch device!

title: Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot are giving everyone the same superpower
dek: That's great; but it also means code is no longer a differentiator. Open source maintainers are already drowning in vibecoded pull requests. Research will feel similar pressure soon: rapid…
body: Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Copilot are giving everyone the same superpower. That's great; but it also means code is no longer a differentiator. Open source maintainers are already drowning in vibecoded pull requests. Research will feel similar pressure soon: rapid prototypes paired with paper-thin evaluations.

But I think the real takeaway is more positive than that. Reducing the barrier of code evens the playing field. And it makes the actual hard parts of research (formulating questions, designing studies, analyzing results) more important, not less.
When everyone is super, the differentiator is what you do with the power, not the power itself.
New blog post: "When Everyone Is Super" - https://lnkd.in/eujFwR2W

body: We are recruiting a new Ph.D. student for an ambitious project on "Human-Centered AI for Augmented and Extended Reality." The position is part of a broader research effort that asks a simple but consequential question: what happens when modern AI meets immersive, always-available XR interfaces?

AI and XR form a powerful pairing. AI brings perception, reasoning, and adaptation; XR brings embodied interaction, spatial context, and presence. Together, they enable interaction paradigms that go well beyond today’s screens—especially as a new generation of headsets and smart glasses moves XR into everyday settings.

The Ph.D. project builds on ongoing work in my Center for Anytime Anywhere Analytics, funded by a Villum Investigator grant from Villum Fonden. The goal is to explore how human-centered AI methods can make XR systems intelligible, usable, and trustworthy in real-world contexts.
The successful candidate will join a large and energetic research group, with multiple postdocs and Ph.D. students, embedded in one of Europe’s leading HCI environments.
Full call and details here (application deadline February 1, 2026):

title: IEEE VIS 2025 has concluded, and as Overall Papers Chairs, Holger Theisel, Melanie Tory, and I can report on two…
dek: The student reviewer program allowed primary reviewers to invite junior PhD students as advisory reviewers. About 20% of primary reviewers participated, generating 99 student reviews across 537…
body: IEEE VIS 2025 has concluded, and as Overall Papers Chairs, Holger Theisel, Melanie Tory, and I can report on two experimental programs we introduced this year.

The student reviewer program allowed primary reviewers to invite junior PhD students as advisory reviewers. About 20% of primary reviewers participated, generating 99 student reviews across 537 submissions. The students received full credit as reviewers, with some earning review distinctions. Our survey of 97 IPC members showed 69.1% support for continuing the program—it exposes previously hidden labor while training the next generation of reviewers.

The public peer review repository publishes anonymized reviews for accepted papers where both authors and reviewers consent. This year, 16 papers qualified, yielding 52 reviews now available on OSF. While more controversial (16.7% wanted to stop it, 65.6% wanted to continue), the repository improves transparency and helps new researchers learn peer review craft. OSF: https://osf.io/s9j5b/

Other findings: Most IPC members found six papers per reviewer appropriate. The reduction from four to three reviewers per paper was acceptable to 61.9% of the committee. Adding an extra week for supplemental materials received near-unanimous support at 83.5%.
Both experimental programs will continue, recommended for three-year evaluation periods before final decisions. The VIS Steering Committee approved both initiatives.
Thank you to our 205 IPC members, the 12 Area Papers Chairs, and especially our assistant Petra Specht, who made all of this possible.
The full blog post with survey details is available at: https://lnkd.in/dbFt9-Ua

title: New paper: "Agentic Visualization - Extracting Agent-based Design Patterns from Visualization Systems"
dek: As part of a team consisting of Vaishali Dhanoa, Anton Wolter, Gabriela Molina León, and Hans-Jörg Schulz, we just posted a new paper on arXiv where we propose "agentic visualization" as the…
body: New paper: "Agentic Visualization - Extracting Agent-based Design Patterns from Visualization Systems"

As part of a team consisting of Vaishali Dhanoa, Anton Wolter, Gabriela Molina León, and Hans-Jörg Schulz, we just posted a new paper on arXiv where we propose "agentic visualization" as the integration of autonomous AI agents with interactive visual analysis systems while balancing computational autonomy with human analytical control.

To determine best practices for such agentic visualization systems, we analyze existing visualization systems that already incorporate automatic or semi-automatic capabilities to extract design patterns as reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems.
The research identifies three core types of such agentic visualization patterns:
* Role patterns: fundamental roles and responsibilities agents can assume within a visualization system, including data foraging, analysis, storytelling, and chart creation;
* Communication patterns: channels for information exchange between agents and human analysts, including insight feeds, progress indication, and provenance; and
* Coordination patterns: workflow dynamics for multi-agent systems, including scouting, swarming, monitoring, and consolidating.
Read the full paper here: https://lnkd.in/dp2xgYtf

dek: The future isn't about embedding data in specific locations: it's about ubiquitous analytics that work anywhere, anytime, across any device. Most analytical tasks don't have a compelling physical…
body: Last week at IEEE VIS Conference 2024, I took a somewhat provocative stance during the "Vogue or Visionary?" panel on situated visualization: While AR-based visualization captures our imagination, I argued that we're solving the wrong problem.

The future isn't about embedding data in specific locations: it's about ubiquitous analytics that work anywhere, anytime, across any device. Most analytical tasks don't have a compelling physical context, and forcing them into one might actually hinder understanding. (Some surely do, but we can't focus undue resources on these edge cases.)

I've expanded on these panel remarks in a new blog post, making the case for flexible, context-aware analytics tools that adapt to users' needs rather than merely their location: https://lnkd.in/dGFkpWdq
Panel website: https://lnkd.in/d9Eajn3H
Thanks to Michelle Borkin, Melanie Tory, and Mackenzie Creamer for inviting me, I very much enjoyed the chance to listen my own voice! 🧐 😉

title: I've been reflecting on our field's focus on replicating real-world experiences
dek: While intuitive, this approach may be limiting our potential to create truly transformative technology.
body: I've been reflecting on our field's focus on replicating real-world experiences. While intuitive, this approach may be limiting our potential to create truly transformative technology.

Instead of chasing perfect emulations of physical experiences, what if we focused on creating tools that complement and enhance human capabilities in unprecedented ways? Consider voice assistants: rather than solely trying to match human conversation, we should emphasize their unique ability to instantly synthesize information from vast knowledge bases.

This shift in perspective aligns with the principles of human-centered AI (HCAI), where the goal isn't to replace human capabilities but to augment them. It's time to move beyond digital replicas and embrace the potential of HCAI tools.

title: Ethical question I'd love to get your take on: is it self-plagiarism to reuse content from your own peer-reviewed…
dek: Obviously, each of the papers will be cited in the dissertation, but not every instance of text reuse would be quoted. The dissertation would also include a contribution statement for each…
body: Ethical question I'd love to get your take on: is it self-plagiarism to reuse content from your own peer-reviewed papers (with co-authors) in your Ph.D. dissertation? (Or, more clearly, is it an allowable form of self-plagiarism or not?)

Obviously, each of the papers will be cited in the dissertation, but not every instance of text reuse would be quoted. The dissertation would also include a contribution statement for each co-author. Chapters might include statements to the effect of "this chapter is based on publication X", with a lot of the original text from the peer-reviewed publication used verbatim.

I have always thought of dissertations as "special" forms of publications that represent the combined works of a student's Ph.D.; after all, if you publish a chapter from your dissertation after receiving your degree, you will cite the dissertation but you won't have to quote extensively every reused passage.
Having to quote or rewrite every single passage seems counterproductive to me, and also effectively penalizes those students with the wherewithal to publish during their Ph.D.s.
How do you navigate this in your work? What advice do you give your Ph.D. students?

title: For all their hype and controversy, generative AI in general—and LLMs in particular—are here to stay
dek: Their potential for helping writers is indisputable. An LLM can generate content, offer new ideas, and help writers overcome writer’s block. However, at the same time, they threaten originality,…
body: For all their hype and controversy, generative AI in general—and LLMs in particular—are here to stay. Their potential for helping writers is indisputable. An LLM can generate content, offer new ideas, and help writers overcome writer’s block. However, at the same time, they threaten originality, raise issues of authenticity, and question the ownership of text. In our recent CHI 2024 paper, we present HaLLMark, an interactive web-based system for human/AI co-writing that uses visualization to address these issues of ownership, authenticity, and human control. Read this blog post to learn more. With Naimul Hoque, Tasfia Mashiat, Bhavya Ghai, Cecilia Shelton, Fanny Chevalier, and Kari Kraus.

title: Back in my 2008 InfoVis paper on ScatterDice, we introduced "query sculpting": iteratively refining faceted queries…
dek: At #ieeevis 2023, Naimul Hoque and I are baaaack for Part Deux: "Aggregate Query Sculpting" (AQS).
body: Back in my 2008 InfoVis paper on ScatterDice, we introduced "query sculpting": iteratively refining faceted queries into multidimensional data. At #ieeevis 2023, Naimul Hoque and I are baaaack for Part Deux: "Aggregate Query Sculpting" (AQS).

Our "Dataopsy: Scalable and Fluid Visual Exploration using Aggregate Query Sculpting" paper both introduces AQS as well as "Dataopsy" (read: autopsy for data; pronounced the same way), our implementation of AQS for web-based and mobile devices.

The AQS idea is simple and "born scalable": start with a single aggregate node (supernode) representing ALL items and then use query operators to explore the data. This idea works for both tabular and relational (graph) data. We suggest six query operations (P^6): pivot, partition, peek, pile, project, and prune. Pivot splits supernodes on a criterion, partition lays out nodes, peek visualizes node contents, pile merges nodes, project starts new canvas, and prune deletes.

Our paper presents two case studies---ML fairness evaluation and screenplay adaptation---and two scenarios---taxi trips in NYC and scientometric analysis of IEEE VIS publications. See the paper for more details.
Naimul Hoque will be presenting the paper on Wed, Oct 25. (He is also on the faculty job market and you should chat with him: https://lnkd.in/deuA6ZrF).

title: If you're like me, you have a sneaking suspicion that visualization is old hat to many statisticians
dek: After all, they were early adopters (and early innovators) in data visualization. At #ieeevis 2023, Dr. eric newburger and I look into this once and for all.
body: If you're like me, you have a sneaking suspicion that visualization is old hat to many statisticians. After all, they were early adopters (and early innovators) in data visualization. At #ieeevis 2023, Dr. eric newburger and I look into this once and for all.

In "Visualization According to Statisticians: An Interview Study on the Role of Visualization for Inferential Statistics", we report on 18 interviews with professional statisticians (avg 19.7 years in role) on their visualization use.

We focused on (1) daily use of visualization, (2) mental models of inferential analysis, and (3) design recommendations for statistical inference using visualizations. Thematic coding of transcripts yielded a wealth of data.

Findings: (1) statisticians generally make extensive use of visualization during all analysis phases; (2) their mental models are mostly visually based; and (3) statisticians tend to abhor dichotomous thinking (thus supporting the use of visualization).
Eric, who is a professional statistician himself formerly at the US Census Bureau, will be presenting this work on Wed, October 25 at #ieeevis. We are looking forward to your feedback!
PDF: https://lnkd.in/eWCVEwzx
arXiv: https://lnkd.in/eFCs2fGZ

title: Smartphones have had a revolutionary impact on blind professionals, essentially putting a screen reader in…
dek: As a result, more than 46% of blind people own one. But how can we use it for accessible visualization? At #ieeevis 2023, Pramod Chundury, Yasmin Reyazuddin, J. Bern Jordan, Jonathan Lazar, and I…
body: Smartphones have had a revolutionary impact on blind professionals, essentially putting a screen reader in everyone's pockets. As a result, more than 46% of blind people own one. But how can we use it for accessible visualization? At #ieeevis 2023, Pramod Chundury, Yasmin Reyazuddin, J. Bern Jordan, Jonathan Lazar, and I will be presenting "TactualPlot: Spatializing Data as Sound using Sensory Substitution for Touchscreen Accessibility". Our goal is to basically turn phones into tactile graphics.

Current smartphones do not provide any form of tactile feedback. So how to achieve this effect? Well, through sound, of course! We call this idea "crossmodal sensory substitution" (CMSS); you use one sense as input (touch) and receive output as another (hearing).

We designed TactualPlot, our CMSS implementation, through three design workshops with Yasmin, our blind collaborator and accessible data expert. We then evaluated it in a limited deployment with two external experts.
The current TactualPlot tool enables "feeling" scatterplots by using your fingertips as sampling regions (like an area cursor).
The talk will be given by Pramod Chundury at IEEE VIS 2023 on Thu, Oct 26.
